newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Gas to oil could revolutionise energy supply.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Gas to oil could revolutionise energy supply.

text.p: The economics of the energy industry could be dramatically altered if new technology to convert natural gas into oil proves economic.

At least three companies -- U.S. giant Exxon Corp, South Africa's Sasol Ltd and a small U.S. firm, Syntroleum Corp -- believe they have overcome the obstacles to make gas-into-oil a commercial proposition.

James Ball, managing partner of Gas Strategies in London, said converting gas into oil could be "an exciting alternative route for commercialising natural gas" although he noted that previous attempts have not proved economic.
NEW TECHNOLOGY COULD FREE UP VAST AMOUNTS OF GAS

A report by New York investment bank Salomon Brothers was even more enthusiastic, saying the commercial production of oil from gas would be "truly revolutionary," as it would result in the opening up of vast numbers of gas fields which are currently considered too far from consuming centres to be economically viable.
"The implication of this new technology is mindboggling.
"It may not only alter the fundamental economic balances of the energy industry, but also has significant implications for global geopolitical alliances and geopolitical conflicts," the report said.

William S. Pintz said in a report published by the East-West Center in Hawaii that the latest technological advances could lead to the exploitation of gas deposits amounting to about half of the world's 5,000 trillion cubic feet (140 trillion cubic metres) of proven reserves that are currently "stranded" or uneconomic.
"It is hard to imagine a development with greater potential impact on supplies and suppliers of clean fossil fuels," Pintz said.
The main advantage of oil over gas is that it is cheaper to transport. It does not have to be placed under high pressure in pipelines or cooled to extremely low temperatures if transported by tanker.
In addition, oil products created from gas are potentially cleaner than conventional oil as they do not contain any sulphur.
The end-products are refinery feedstock or so-called middle distillates -- kerosene, diesel and gas oil -- for which world demand is rising fast.
SOUTH AFRICA A PIONEER OF GAS INTO OIL
The idea of converting natural gas into oil is far from new, having been invented by German scientists in the 1920s, but until now the so-called Fischer-Tropsch process has been extremely expensive.

South Africa is the only country which produces "synfuels" or synthetic fuels on a large scale, having been forced to do so when the country was under an international oil embargo due to its apartheid policies.
But the process depended on heavy state subsidies and South Africa's synfuels industry was expected to die a natural death now the country is no longer subject to sanctions.
However, after producing "synfuels" from coal for 40 years, Sasol has for the last four years been producing oil from gas commercially, with output now running at 2,500 barrels per day (bpd).

Both Sasol and Exxon say they have made technical advances that make the process economically viable, and both companies have been holding talks with Qatar on producing oil from gas in the Gulf state which has some of the world's biggest gas reserves.
EXXON, SASOL, MAY PRODUCE OIL FROM GAS IN QATAR
Sasol envisages output of 20,000 bpd in Qatar, while a Qatar General Petroleum Corp official said the Exxon project would use one billion cubic feet per day to produce about 100,000 bpd of oil.
Qatari Energy Minister Abdullah bin Hamad al-Attiyah put the cost of the project at $1.2 billion and said in February that a memorandum of understanding would be signed soon.
This project would be in addition to plans for Qatar to export 12 million tonnes per year of liquefied natural gas by the year 2000.

An Exxon spokesman declined to comment on the Qatari figures but said its technology was aimed at producing between 50,000 and 100,000 bpd. He stressed that no final agreement with Qatar had been reached although a feasibility study had been completed.
Exxon says that "given the right technology gas into oil can be competitive at recent prevailing oil prices," while Sasol says its process is "commercially proven."
In addition, Tulsa, Oklahoma-based Syntroleum has developed its own technology to produce oil from gas, which, like Exxon's and Sasol's, is based on the 70-year-old Fischer-Tropsch process.
AT LAST, OIL FROM GAS MAY BE COMMERCIAL
Syntroleum says its version of the Fischer-Tropsch process can produce oil from gas at an oil price of below $20 a barrel and at a capital cost of $12,000 to $27,000 per barrel of daily capacity.

Salomon Brothers said that at the lower end of this range, gas-to-oil "would be highly competitive with current grass roots refinery capital costs," and that LNG projects had a capital cost of $30,000 to $40,000 per barrel-day of capacity.
Syntroleum says its process is economical on a small scale, and that only two percent of the world's gas fields outside North America are suitable for a large, 50,000 bpd gas-to-oil plant.
"At plant capacities as small as 5,000 bpd, the Syntroleum Process offers a potential solution for almost 40 percent of the world's gas fields, which hold over 95 percent of the world's natural gas.
"The minimum economical size is expected to drop to around 2,000 bpd in the near future," said Syntroleum president Mark Agee last October.

Syntroleum says it has cut the cost of the most expensive part of the synfuel process, the production of so-called "synthesis gas," an intermediate stage in which the company uses air rather than the pure oxygen which is normally used.

The nitrogen-diluted syngas is produced in an autothermal reformer that uses a nickel-based catalyst and is then passed through Fischer-Tropsch reactors that unlike in other versions incorporate nitrogen into the process without impairing performance.
Syntroleum says its aim is to "continue to drive capital costs down until a natural gas refinery can be built for less than a crude oil refinery."
Syntroleum in April signed a licensing deal with Atlantic Richfield Co, after signing similar agreements with Texaco Inc and Marathon Oil Co.
ARCO senior vice-president Skip Bilhartz said, "We are very enthusiastic about the opportunities for applying this technology to ARCO's gas reserves around the world."

ARCO says this could include Alaska, which according to Salomon Brothers has "unbooked" gas reserves (deposits that are currently not considered economically viable) totalling 25-30 trillion cubic feet (tcf).
Salomon Brothers says ARCO's net unbooked reserves in Alaska total 10 tcf or more, and the opening up of these deposits "could potentially double ARCO's gas reserves in one fell swoop."
NEW TECHNOLOGY COULD BE THREAT TO OIL PRICES
Ball of Gas Strategies said that "if gas-to-oil happens on an enormous scale, it would be a threat to the oil industry and to oil prices."

But there had been false dawns before, he said, referring to a commercially unsuccessful attempt by Mobil Corp in New Zealand in the 1980s and a Royal Dutch/Shell plant that has been producing 12,500 bpd of middle distillates from gas at Bintulu, Malaysia since 1993.

However, the Shell plant depended on producing small quantities of highly valued specialist products such as lubricants to be profitable, and the market for these was too limited to form the basis of a whole new industry, Ball said.
A Shell spokesman said there were no plans to expand the Bintulu plant or build further such projects.

Ball also said gas-into-oil potentially "creates a lot more refined, sellable oil. If those markets are finite, we can't assume we can stuff highly valuable products into them without an effect on the oil price...
"If the middle distillates market is glutted it may in fact drive itself out of business."
But Ball said he was encouraged by Sasol's plans in particular "as they have more experience in the field than anyone else...I think they might be onto a winner."
